readings.title: A seat at the evening table
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
On her first evening at the neighbourhood reading group, Lin chose the chair nearest the door. She had recently returned to study and worried that everyone else would have clever things to say. The group was discussing a short story about a woman who missed a train. Lin had read it twice, but when the leader asked for opinions, she kept her notebook closed.

The first speaker talked about the writer's style. Another compared the story with a novel Lin had never heard of. Then an older man asked a simple question: why had the woman arrived so early if she disliked waiting? Nobody answered immediately. Lin remembered a sentence in which the woman checked her watch before leaving home. She read it aloud and suggested that the character feared being late more than she disliked waiting.

Her comment did not settle the question. Someone pointed to a different sentence, and the group considered another explanation. What surprised Lin was that disagreement did not end the conversation. It made everyone look more closely at the page. By the end of the evening, she had written down several questions instead of a list of correct answers.

On the bus home, Lin thought about the chair she had chosen. She had expected the group to reward people who knew the most books. Instead, one careful observation had given her a way to participate. She still wanted to learn the terms that other members used, but they no longer seemed like tickets she needed before entering the discussion.

At the next meeting, Lin sat farther from the door. When a new member apologised for having little experience, she opened her notebook. There was a question she had not been able to answer, and she wanted to know what the newcomer thought about it.

readings.title: The price of convenience
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
When a small office began ordering lunches in reusable containers, the arrangement seemed simple. Meals arrived at noon, empty containers went into a box, and the delivery company collected them the next morning. The office expected to reduce the number of disposable packages in its bins without asking employees to change their routines very much.

During the first month, however, containers regularly went missing. Some remained on desks; others were taken home and forgotten. The company charged a deposit for each one that was not returned. A manager suggested putting a large warning beside the collection box. An employee who often worked from home proposed a different explanation: the system assumed that everyone would be in the office on two consecutive days.

That detail changed the discussion. A person who bought lunch on Tuesday might not return until Friday. Keeping the container clean at home was possible, but remembering to carry it back required an extra step. The employees were not necessarily opposed to reuse. The return arrangement simply fitted some working patterns better than others.

The office moved the collection box beside the main exit and allowed returns throughout the week. The company agreed to collect less often, provided that enough containers were available for the next delivery. A brief reminder appeared in the ordering message, where people would see it before choosing lunch. Returns improved, although a few containers still had to be replaced.

The change involved a trade-off: more containers were needed to keep the system running. Yet the office considered that cost alongside the reduction in disposable packaging, rather than pretending that reuse was effortless. A convenient service can make a better habit easier, but convenience must be designed around the people who use it. Otherwise, a small forgotten task may defeat an attractive environmental promise.
knowledgePoints: 阅读理解：日常行为与服务设计

readings.title: Directions remembered
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A geography teacher asked her adult students to try two ways of learning an unfamiliar route. Half the class studied a simple map for five minutes. The others received a sequence of written instructions, such as “turn left at the bakery”. Both groups then walked to a small public garden without using phones. A tutor accompanied each group, but offered help only if someone became lost.

Most students reached the garden successfully. Those following the written instructions often arrived sooner because they did not pause to work out the direction of the next street. If the exercise had ended there, the teacher might have concluded that the instructions were the more useful tool. Instead, she asked everyone to explain how the garden was positioned in relation to the station.

The map readers generally found this second task easier. Several could describe streets they had not actually walked along. Some students who had followed instructions remembered the bakery clearly but could not say whether the station lay north or south of the garden. They had learned a sequence of actions rather than an overall arrangement of places.

The teacher warned against making too much of the result. The groups were small, and some students had more experience reading maps. The exercise did not prove that one method was always better. A visitor carrying heavy bags might reasonably prefer quick directions. Someone planning several journeys across the same area might benefit from seeing its wider layout.

For the final activity, students combined the two methods. They marked a route on a map and added short notes at difficult turns. This was not a competition between old and new ways of travelling. It was a reminder to choose information according to the task: reaching a place efficiently and understanding how places connect are related goals, but they are not identical.

readings.title: A useful silence
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
In many workplaces, a quick reply is treated as a sign of cooperation. Messages arrive throughout the day, and people answer them between other tasks. For simple questions, this can be useful. Yet a person preparing a careful report may find that a series of small interruptions consumes more attention than the messages themselves appear to require.

At one design office, employees were allowed to reserve two quiet hours each week. During that period, they could close their messaging application and put a small card on their desk. The card did not mean that colleagues were unwelcome. It showed when the employee expected to be available again and named another person who could handle urgent requests.

The arrangement initially worried some team members. They thought problems might remain unnoticed or that quiet hours would be used to avoid difficult conversations. To address these concerns, the office distinguished between urgent issues and matters that could wait. A broken delivery arrangement still required an immediate response; a suggestion about the next month's meeting usually did not. Teams could also choose different quiet periods so that someone remained available.

After several weeks, staff described mixed results. Writers and designers valued the uninterrupted time, while reception staff had fewer opportunities to use it. The manager therefore asked each team to develop an equivalent way of protecting attention, rather than requiring identical schedules. Reception workers arranged short periods away from the desk for administrative tasks, with colleagues covering their places.

The aim was not to create a silent office or make rapid communication seem unimportant. It was to recognise that availability has a cost as well as a benefit. Cooperation sometimes means answering immediately; at other times, it means allowing a colleague to finish a demanding piece of work. Clear expectations help people tell the difference without interpreting every delayed reply as a refusal to help.

grammar.explanation: would rather+主语+过去式表示希望某人现在或将来做某事，read 的过去式拼写仍为 read，选 A。

translation.stem:
Translate the following passage into Chinese:
People often describe curiosity as a personal quality, but the setting in which we learn also matters. A question may remain unasked when a learner expects an impatient reply. In a welcoming discussion, the same question can reveal a difficulty shared by several people. This does not mean that every idea is equally convincing. Participants still need to explain their reasons and pay attention to evidence. The aim is to make uncertainty a useful starting point rather than something to hide. When people can admit what they do not understand, they give themselves and others a better chance to learn something new.
translation.explanation: 参考译文供自评。注意 setting 指学习环境，shared by several people 修饰 difficulty，rather than 连接两种对待不确定性的态度。按意义完整、语言准确和表达自然评分。
translation.referenceAnswer: 人们常把好奇心描述为一种个人品质，但我们所处的学习环境也很重要。如果学习者预料会得到不耐烦的回答，一个问题就可能始终没有被提出。在友好的讨论中，同一个问题可能揭示好几个人共有的困惑。这并不意味着每一种想法都同样令人信服。参与者仍须说明理由，并重视证据。目的在于让不确定性成为有用的起点，而不是需要掩饰的东西。当人们能够承认自己不懂什么时，也就让自己和他人更有机会学到新知识。

criteria.name: 意义完整
criteria.description: 准确传达全部主要信息与逻辑关系，不遗漏重要内容。

criteria.name: 语言准确
criteria.description: 词义、时态和指代处理准确，无严重误译。

criteria.name: 表达自然
criteria.description: 中文通顺，段落衔接清楚。

writing.stem: Write at least 100 words in English to invite a colleague to a lunchtime learning group. Explain the purpose of the group, describe what participants will do, and make clear how someone with little experience can join.
writing.explanation: 范文覆盖活动目的、时间地点、参与方式和对新成员的支持，供考生依任务完成、组织连贯与语言运用三项自评。
writing.sampleAnswer:
Dear Alex,
I would like to invite you to our lunchtime learning group next Wednesday. We meet in the small conference room from twelve thirty to one. The purpose is to share useful ideas from everyday work and discuss questions that we have not yet solved.
At the next meeting, each person can bring a short example of something they have learned recently. We will spend a few minutes listening, then ask questions and compare different approaches. You do not need to prepare a formal presentation or have any special knowledge. If you prefer, you can simply listen at your first meeting.
I remember you mentioning a difficulty with organising project notes, and your experience could give us a valuable starting point. Please let me know if you would like to come.
Best wishes,
Chris

criteria.name: 任务完成
criteria.description: 覆盖全部写作要点，内容具体且相关。

criteria.name: 组织连贯
criteria.description: 段落清楚，衔接自然，格式适合任务。

criteria.name: 语言运用
criteria.description: 词汇和语法基本准确，有适当句式变化。
